Introduction to MS Word

Microsoft Word is a word-processing application and a core component of the Microsoft Office suite. It is used to create, edit, format and print documents such as letters, reports, resumes and essays. The default file format of modern versions of Word is .docx, while older versions used .doc. Microsoft Office was first released in 1990 for Macintosh and in 1992 for Windows.

Formatting in MS Word

Formatting improves the appearance and readability of a document. It is broadly divided into three levels. Character formatting changes the appearance of individual characters and includes font, font size, bold, italic, underline, font colour and effects such as superscript and subscript. Paragraph formatting applies to whole paragraphs and includes alignment, line spacing, indentation, spacing before and after a paragraph, and bullets and numbering. Page formatting controls the layout of the whole document and includes page size, margins, orientation (portrait or landscape), headers and footers, and page numbers.

Common paragraph alignments are left, centre, right and justified. In justified alignment, text is spread evenly between the left and right margins. The Format Painter tool copies formatting from one part of a document and applies it to another part.

Tables in MS Word

A table organises information into rows and columns. The intersection of a row and a column is called a cell. A table can be inserted from the Insert tab, and rows, columns and cells can be added or deleted afterwards. The Table Tools tabs, Design and Layout, provide options for table styles, borders, shading, merging cells, splitting cells and sorting table contents. Text in a table can be converted to a table, and a table can also be converted back to text.

Mail Merge

Mail Merge is a feature used to produce many personalised documents, such as letters, envelopes, labels or certificates, from one main document and one data source. The main document contains the fixed text, while the data source, such as an Excel worksheet or an Access table, contains the variable information, for example names and addresses. A merge field is a placeholder in the main document that is replaced by data from the data source for each recipient.

The standard mail merge process is as follows:

  • Step 1: Start Mail Merge and select the document type, such as letters, envelopes or labels.
  • Step 2: Select Recipients and choose or create the data source.
  • Step 3: Insert Merge Fields into the main document at the required places.
  • Step 4: Preview Results to check how each merged document will look.
  • Step 5: Finish and Merge, either by printing the merged documents or by merging them into a new document or email messages.

Mail Merge is found on the Mailings tab in Microsoft Word. It saves time and avoids errors when the same letter must be sent to many people with only small personal details changed.

bodyText:
Introduction to MS Excel

Microsoft Excel is a spreadsheet application in the Microsoft Office suite. It is used for calculations, data analysis, budgeting, record keeping and presenting data in charts. An Excel file is called a workbook, and a workbook contains one or more worksheets. A worksheet is divided into rows and columns, and the intersection of a row and a column is called a cell. Each cell is identified by its cell address, which combines its column letter and row number, for example B5. The default file extension of modern Excel workbooks is .xlsx, while older versions used .xls.

Formulas and Functions

Every formula in Excel begins with an equal sign (=). A formula may contain cell references, numbers, operators and functions. The arithmetic operators are addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*) and division (/). A function is a built-in formula that performs a specific calculation, for example SUM adds a range of numbers and AVERAGE calculates their mean. Cell references may be relative, absolute or mixed; an absolute reference uses dollar signs, for example $A$1, so that it does not change when copied to another cell.

Charts in MS Excel

A chart is a graphical representation of worksheet data that makes trends and comparisons easier to understand. Common chart types include column charts, bar charts, line charts and pie charts. A column chart compares values across categories, a line chart shows trends over time, and a pie chart shows the proportion of each part to the whole. Charts are created from the Insert tab after selecting the data to be charted, and they update automatically when the source data changes.

Sorting and Filtering

Sorting arranges data in a chosen order. Data can be sorted in ascending order, from smallest to largest or A to Z, or in descending order, from largest to smallest or Z to A. Sorting can be done on a single column or on multiple levels, for example sorting first by department and then by name. Filtering, by contrast, temporarily hides rows that do not meet a condition, without deleting them, so that only the required records are visible. Both sorting and filtering are found on the Data tab in Excel.

bodyText:
Introduction to MS PowerPoint

Microsoft PowerPoint is a presentation application in the Microsoft Office suite. It is used to create slide-based presentations for teaching, business meetings, seminars and conferences. A PowerPoint file is called a presentation, and it is made up of slides. Each slide can contain text, images, tables, charts, audio and video. The default file extension of modern PowerPoint presentations is .pptx, while older versions used .ppt.

Slides and Slide Layouts

A slide is a single page of a presentation. A new slide is inserted from the Home tab or with Ctrl+M. A slide layout is a pre-arranged arrangement of placeholders, which are boxes that hold text, pictures, tables or charts. Common layouts include Title Slide, Title and Content, and Blank. A slide master controls the overall design of all slides in a presentation, including background, fonts and placeholder positions, so that a change to the master is reflected throughout the presentation.

Transitions and Animations

A transition is a visual effect applied when moving from one slide to the next, for example Fade, Push or Wipe. An animation is an effect applied to an individual object on a slide, such as text or a picture appearing, for example by fading in or flying in. The distinction is frequently tested: transitions act between slides, while animations act on objects within a slide. Both are used sparingly in professional presentations, so that effects support the message rather than distract from it.

Templates and Themes

A template is a pre-designed presentation file that provides a ready-made layout, colour scheme, fonts and background, so that the user only needs to add content. A theme is a set of colours, fonts and effects that gives a presentation a consistent look. PowerPoint provides built-in templates and themes, and users can also create and save their own templates. The file extension for a PowerPoint template is .potx. A slide show can be started from the beginning with F5, and from the current slide with Shift+F5; pressing Esc ends a slide show.

bodyText:
Introduction to MS Access

Microsoft Access is a database management system (DBMS) in the Microsoft Office suite. It is used to store, organise, retrieve and manage large amounts of structured data, for example student records, customer lists and inventory. A database is an organised collection of related data. The default file extension of modern Access databases is .accdb, while older versions used .mdb. Access is a relational database management system (RDBMS), which means data is stored in related tables rather than in a single flat list.

Basic Database Concepts

A table is the basic unit of a database and stores data in rows and columns. Each row in a table is called a record, and each column is called a field. A field holds one type of information, for example a student name or a roll number, and a record holds all the information about one item, for example one student. Common field data types in Access include Short Text for short text values, Number for numeric values, Date/Time for dates and times, Currency for monetary values, and Yes/No for true or false values.

A primary key is a field, or a combination of fields, that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A primary key cannot contain duplicate values and cannot be left blank. A foreign key is a field in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, and it is used to link related tables together. Relationships between tables are commonly one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many; in a one-to-many relationship, one record in the first table can be related to many records in the second table, for example one teacher to many students.

Objects in MS Access

An Access database is built from objects. Tables store the data. Queries retrieve, filter and analyse data from one or more tables according to criteria set by the user, without changing the stored data itself. Forms provide a user-friendly screen for entering, viewing and editing data. Reports present data in a formatted, printable form, for example a mark sheet or a summary report. Macros and modules provide automation and programming facilities in more advanced databases.

Access uses Structured Query Language (SQL) behind the scenes for queries. A simple query in SQL selects fields from a table, for example SELECT Name FROM Students. Understanding tables, records, fields, primary keys and queries is the foundation for PPSC questions on databases.
